# Lessons of glibc-crustify

Rules that hold for this campaign alone, as `evolution`'s Lessons section describes. Every
run reads them before its first step.

## A batch's gates run with no build variant

**Rule.** libc is the system's, so `build.json` has no variants, and this tree has no
`cargo-variant` script. A batch runs its gates directly, each build in a target dir of its
own under `crustify/tmp/`:

- campaign mode: `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=<plain | asan-ubsan | tsan>` set on every
  `cargo` command that builds the tests, which then regenerate the bindings and check them
  against the committed ones;
- format: `cargo +<the workspace's nightly> fmt --all -- --check`, since `rustfmt.toml`
  uses nightly-only options;
- ASan: on that nightly, `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, with
  `RUSTFLAGS="-Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"`, and the same flags in
  `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, without which the doctests fail to link against the ASan runtime; TSan:
  the same with `-Zsanitizer=thread` and `-Zbuild-std`. They instrument the Rust alone,
  since the system's glibc is not instrumented, so TSan sees no race inside glibc. The host
  has no `llvm-symbolizer` on its `PATH`, so a sanitizer trace a report carries is
  symbolized with `ASAN_OPTIONS=external_symbolizer_path=/usr/bin/addr2line`;
- coverage: Rust only, measured as the parent's `crustify/scripts/coverage/baseline.sh`
  does, over a scratch copy without `c/`. Its `report.py` rejects the scope, since
  `llvm-cov` prints this tree's file names relative to `src/`, so the `TOTAL` line is read
  from `llvm-cov report` itself. The compile-fail suite fails in the marked copy, which
  only a nightly builds, and it covers nothing.
- a wave's and a module's end gates: `testing-gates`' `end-gates`, with `--stages
  plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri` and with `--runner` set to a script in `crustify/tmp/`. Given
  `<variant> <cargo args>`, the script runs `cargo` with the flags above, adding
  `--target-dir` under the worktree's `crustify/tmp/` so that every snapshot reuses one
  build per variant. Miri takes `--stage-env miri:CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=plain` and
  `--stage-env miri:CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<worktree>/crustify/tmp/target-miri`.

**Evidence.** wave-2/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/genops.c`) worked these out by hand.
wave-2/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, wrote the `end-gates` runner by hand too.
wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`) found that the `struct_tm_h` doctest fails to
link under ASan without `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, and passes with it.
wave-4/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/stdio.c`) found the doctests failing to link under ASan with
`RUSTFLAGS` alone (`undefined symbol: __asan_init`), and passing with `RUSTDOCFLAGS`.
wave-4/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, found its reproducer's ASan trace printed as bare
addresses, and symbolized through `addr2line`.

**Scope.** Every batch until the tree gets a variant script.

## A threaded stream test writes a file stream, not an `open_memstream` one

**Rule.** A test that writes one stream from several threads, to check that its writes
hold the stream's lock, opens a file stream (`fopen`), whose buffer glibc allocates once.
An `open_memstream` stream grows its buffer with `malloc` and `free` inside each write,
under the stream's lock. TSan intercepts those calls but not glibc's lock, which is an
uninstrumented futex, so it reports every two threads' reallocations as a data race in
`free` (`_IO_str_overflow`), and the suite fails under TSan though the writes are
serialized. A test with one writing thread may use either.

**Evidence.** wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`):
`writes_from_threads_never_interleave` over `open_memstream` was reported under TSan, and was
clean over `fopen` in five runs. It still fails without the binding's `flockfile`, with
interleaved lines over `fopen` and a glibc abort over `open_memstream`.

**Scope.** Every TSan run over tests that share a C stream between threads, `stderr`'s
(wave 4) included.

## An operation that takes a stream's lock refuses a stream without one

**Rule.** An operation bound on `FileRef` that takes the stream's lock with `flockfile`, or
tries it with `ftrylockfile`, first checks that the stream has a lock (`_lock` non-null), as
`FileRef::print`'s `has_lock` does (`src/libc/stdio_common/fprintf.rs`). If it has none,
the operation returns `io::ErrorKind::Unsupported`, writes nothing and leaves `errno` alone.
glibc's lock routines dereference `_lock` without checking it. glibc's own stdio routines
skip the lock on such a stream, and Rust cannot do the same without breaking `FileRef`'s
`Sync`. Every stream a program opens has a lock, as do the standard streams. The stream
glibc hands the handler of a `register_printf_specifier` conversion has none, and it
honours `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract.

**Evidence.** wave-3/batch-1/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s module pass): finding
`contracts/ffi_import/print-locks-a-stream-without-a-lock`, whose reproducer dies with a
SEGV in `flockfile` under ASan on `53dd776`. The unit test
`a_stream_without_a_lock_is_refused` uses the `in_printf_handler` fixture
(`tests/fixtures/stream_unit.rs`), which gives later operations that stream to test against.

**Scope.** Every later operation on `FileRef` that locks the stream, `stderr`'s (wave 4)
included, as long as `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract admits every open stream.

  from `llvm-cov report` itself. The compile-fail suite fails in the marked copy, which
  only a nightly builds, and it covers nothing.
- a wave's and a module's end gates: `testing-gates`' `end-gates`, with `--stages
  plain,asan-ubsan,tsan,miri` and with `--runner` set to a script in `crustify/tmp/`. Given
  `<variant> <cargo args>`, the script runs `cargo` with the flags above, adding
  `--target-dir` under the worktree's `crustify/tmp/` so that every snapshot reuses one
  build per variant. Miri takes `--stage-env miri:CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=plain` and
  `--stage-env miri:CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<worktree>/crustify/tmp/target-miri`.

**Evidence.** wave-2/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/genops.c`) worked these out by hand.
wave-2/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, wrote the `end-gates` runner by hand too.
wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`) found that the `struct_tm_h` doctest fails to
link under ASan without `RUSTDOCFLAGS`, and passes with it.
wave-4/batch-0/run-1 (`libio/stdio.c`) found the doctests failing to link under ASan with
`RUSTFLAGS` alone (`undefined symbol: __asan_init`), and passing with `RUSTDOCFLAGS`.
wave-4/batch-1/run-1, its module pass, found its reproducer's ASan trace printed as bare
addresses, and symbolized through `addr2line`.

**Scope.** Every batch until the tree gets a variant script.

## A threaded stream test writes a file stream, not an `open_memstream` one

**Rule.** A test that writes one stream from several threads, to check that its writes
hold the stream's lock, opens a file stream (`fopen`), whose buffer glibc allocates once.
An `open_memstream` stream grows its buffer with `malloc` and `free` inside each write,
under the stream's lock. TSan intercepts those calls but not glibc's lock, which is an
uninstrumented futex, so it reports every two threads' reallocations as a data race in
`free` (`_IO_str_overflow`), and the suite fails under TSan though the writes are
serialized. A test with one writing thread may use either.

**Evidence.** wave-3/batch-0/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`):
`writes_from_threads_never_interleave` over `open_memstream` was reported under TSan, and was
clean over `fopen` in five runs. It still fails without the binding's `flockfile`, with
interleaved lines over `fopen` and a glibc abort over `open_memstream`.

**Scope.** Every TSan run over tests that share a C stream between threads, `stderr`'s
(wave 4) included.

## An operation that takes a stream's lock refuses a stream without one

**Rule.** An operation bound on `FileRef` that takes the stream's lock with `flockfile`, or
tries it with `ftrylockfile`, first checks that the stream has a lock (`_lock` non-null), as
`FileRef::print`'s `has_lock` does (`src/libc/stdio_common/fprintf.rs`). If it has none,
the operation returns `io::ErrorKind::Unsupported`, writes nothing and leaves `errno` alone.
glibc's lock routines dereference `_lock` without checking it. glibc's own stdio routines
skip the lock on such a stream, and Rust cannot do the same without breaking `FileRef`'s
`Sync`. Every stream a program opens has a lock, as do the standard streams. The stream
glibc hands the handler of a `register_printf_specifier` conversion has none, and it
honours `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract.

**Evidence.** wave-3/batch-1/run-1 (`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s module pass): finding
`contracts/ffi_import/print-locks-a-stream-without-a-lock`, whose reproducer dies with a
SEGV in `flockfile` under ASan on `53dd776`. The unit test
`a_stream_without_a_lock_is_refused` uses the `in_printf_handler` fixture
(`tests/fixtures/stream_unit.rs`), which gives later operations that stream to test against.

**Scope.** Every later operation on `FileRef` that locks the stream, `stderr`'s (wave 4)
included, as long as `FileRef::from_ptr`'s contract admits every open stream.
----

Fill in as many answers as you want before starting Crustify. It will ask only
for campaign decisions that remain unresolved.

# Mandatory questions

## Campaign

1. **Which repository and revision should this campaign use?** (`id: source`)
   - Answer: `https://sourceware.org/git/glibc.git`, `glibc-2.39` (`ef321e23c2`): the
     `c/` submodule. The release the parent campaign, `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings`, links:
     the system's glibc, package `libc6-dev 2.39-0ubuntu8.9`, whose distribution patches
     `crustify/artifacts/dependencies.json` of the parent records. Side campaign of
     `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings` and of `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings`, which links the
     same glibc 2.39.

2. **Should this campaign port the C implementation to Rust, or create safe
   Rust wrappers?** (`id: campaign`)
   - Answer: `wrap`

3. **What should this campaign target: a named subset of modules, or a named
   subset of functions and types, or the whole target repo? You can define them
   now or we can brainstorm them during the live session. You can also let the
   orchestrator decide.** (`id: scope`)
   - Answer: what the parent campaigns consume from libc, the entities their dependency
     records count: for `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings`, `struct tm` (`libavutil/bprint.c`,
     `libavutil/parseutils.c`) and `FILE` (`libavformat/dump.c`); for
     `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings`, 871 functions, 95 structs and 2 globals, counted per
     module over its 168 modules that use libc; growing as the parents' waves need more

4. **Which model and billing should do the translation work?**
   (`id: translate-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, the parent
     `libgit2-crustify`'s answer since 2026-11-13, in the current template's format:
     `<claude | codex>, <subscription | api>[, proxy: openrouter][, args: ...]`
   - Format: `<provider/model, api | subscription>`, e.g.
     `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5, api`. The provider is the first
     segment and selects both the billing rate table and the backend CLI.
     Supported providers:
     - `anthropic/<model>` — Anthropic direct, driven by Claude Code;
     - `openai/<model>` — OpenAI direct, driven by Codex;
     - `openrouter/<vendor>/<model>` — OpenRouter, which resells every vendor
       behind one key, so the vendor segment picks the CLI: `anthropic/*` is
       driven by Claude Code and everything else by Codex. OpenRouter
       supports `api` billing only.

5. **Do you want agentic review after translated work lands? If so, which
   model and billing should perform each review?** (`id: review-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5`, after each wave

6. **Should I run fully autonomously end to end?** (`id: autonomy`)
   - Answer: `no`

# Optional questions

Unanswered optional questions use their defaults.

## Campaign execution

7. **Which model and billing should plan the campaign, and how many planner runs
   should it make? Each run emits what the plan lacks and corrects what the runs
   before it committed.** (`id: plan-agent`)
   - Answer: `claude, api, proxy: openrouter, args: --model claude-opus-5-5, runs: 1` for an
     advance that names its entities; the parent's answer otherwise.
   - By default: the translation model and billing, 2 runs.

8. **Should the campaign use the default batching and parallelism settings, or
   customize them?** (`id: workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`, the parent's answer.

9. **What batch caps should review agents use? We recommend the same caps as
   translation by default.** (`id: review-workload`)
   - Answer: `assistant's choice`, the parent's answer.

10. **Which objectives should review agents review for? By default, every one the
    reviewer offers.** (`id: review-objectives`)
    - Answer: `all`
    - Without `fix`, reviewers report and reproduce what they find but patch nothing.

11. **Which sanitizers should the campaign build and test under? By default, every one
    the toolchain supports.** (`id: sanitizers`)
    - Answer: `asan-ubsan, tsan, bsan`, instrumenting the Rust; the system's glibc they
      link is not instrumented. MSan is not built.
    - From 2026-11-13, as in the parent: BSan runs over the whole workspace, and as a
      regression gate, only once before each ship point; otherwise an agent may run it on
      small things, the tests its own work adds or changes and a review's reproducer,
      each test named and under a `timeout`. This departs from the `testing-gates`
      skill's Regressions section.
    - Miri needs no build and is always on.

12. **How should the target be configured: which of its build features should be
    enabled or disabled?** (`id: target-config`)
    - Answer: none: libc is the system's, which the parent and every other library on
      the host link, so glibc is not built; `c/` is its source, for reading its behaviour,
      and the raw bindings are generated from the host's headers.
    - By default: the target's default configuration, with deprecated features disabled.

## Evolution and shipping

- **How far may the campaign evolve Crustify and its tools?** (`id: evolution`)
  - Answer: `evolve`, on the parent's working branches (`libgit2-crustify/devel` of each
    component), the parent `libgit2-crustify`'s answer: a side campaign's settings are its
    parent's.
- **At which points should the wrapper ship?** (`id: ship`)
  - Answer: with the parent: the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins when the parent
    ships, each with the user's approval.

## Commits

13. **Which git identity should the campaign's commits carry: an author, and any
    co-authors? By default, Crustify's own, `crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the
    GitHub account `crustify-ai`), as the author, with no co-author.** (`id: identity`)
    - Answer: `author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>, co-authors: crustify
      <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (the GitHub account `crustify-ai`)

Answer these approval-gate questions only if question 6 is answered `no`.

---
name: analysis
description: "How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported: what is inspected, what the analysis establishes and how its findings shape the Rust. Read before binding or porting any item, and when reviewing either."
---

# Item analysis

How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported. The analysis is the same
for both: what it establishes shapes the binding or port that follows.

## 1. Scope

Each item is analysed from its source declarations and definitions, its dependency closure,
its callers, its field touchers and its existing Rust consumers. For every pointer field,
argument and return, every code path that stores, transfers, clones, retains or frees it is
inspected.

## 2. Findings

The analysis establishes:

- ownership and transfer direction;
- shared or mutable access;
- nullability;
- scalar, array, or other cardinality;
- type erasure and known element types;
- borrow and keepalive relationships;
- address retention: whether C keeps an object's address beyond the call that receives it,
  to read it, call back with it or free it;
- construction, clone, and destruction paths;
- states and transitions: the states each type's objects pass through, and the calls that
  move them between states, in the orders C allows;
- out-parameters: the pointer arguments a function only writes through;
- string encodings, where a string is known to hold text or a path; and
- failure reporting: the status or sentinel returns and the error state beside the call
  through which a function fails, and the outcomes its callers treat as ordinary.

Observed behaviour overrides names and comments. A distinction the analysis establishes is
preserved in Rust rather than flattened into a copy of an ambiguous C signature.
---
name: binding
description: "How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding: the safe boundary every binding keeps, and the routes binding-types and binding-symbols give types and symbols. Read before binding any item, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.
---
name: binding-symbols
description: "How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding, binding's symbol route: functions and what their signatures carry, globals, function pointers, macros and lifecycle strategies. Read before binding any symbol, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Binding symbols

How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding: the symbol route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section and reaches the types
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md) binds. [`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md) starts from it.

## 1. Functions

A function is bound as a `pub fn`; it is a `pub unsafe fn` only when no safe type-level
contract can express its caller obligation. Its FFI call, and the raw pointers it
reconstructs for it, sit in its module's `ffi_import` region, as the
[conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes.

Its signature follows the analysis's findings, each argument and return taking the safe
form of what it names:

- **Out-parameters.** A pointer the function only writes through, to hand back a result,
  is part of the return, several of them a tuple, present only in the outcome in which the
  function writes it.
- **Buffers.** A pointer and the count that bounds it are one slice, the count taken from
  it; a buffer the function fills returns the part it filled.
- **Strings.** A NUL-terminated string the function borrows for the call is a borrowed C
  string, or the Rust string or path type of the encoding the analysis establishes,
  converted at the call, an interior NUL rejected before it. A returned string is a borrow
  tied to what keeps it alive, or an owner over its releaser where the caller frees it.
- **Nullability.** A nullable pointer is an `Option`.
- **Errors.** A function that can fail returns a `Result`, its failure read from the error
  convention the analysis establishes: a status return, a sentinel return, or error state
  the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it, before another call into
  the library can replace it. A return that reports only success is not returned, and an
  outcome its C callers treat as ordinary, such as an exhausted iteration or an absent
  entry, is part of the success value. Each error convention has one error type, carrying
  what the convention reports, `errno`'s being `std::io::Error`.
- **Variadics.** A variadic function is bound through fixed-arity forms: one that formats
  its arguments takes the formatted message, passed to a `"%s"` format, and any other is
  one function per argument list its callers use. A `va_list` function is reached only
  through its variadic sibling.

A `static inline` function a header defines is bound as an exported one is: it is
allowlisted, and called through the raw binding generated for it, as
[`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes. The exception is a short
one whose whole implementation is in the header, which may be ported instead, to save the
cost of an FFI call, unless what it does depends on the build's features or configuration.
A reimplementation is a port, as [`porting`](../../porting/SKILL.md) describes, and is
annotated `Replaces`, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Anchors section describes.

Moved (exclusively or refcounted), borrowed (immutably or mutably), nullable, scalar and
array variants are separate functions when one signature cannot express every valid

# Item analysis

How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported. The analysis is the same
for both: what it establishes shapes the binding or port that follows.

## 1. Scope

Each item is analysed from its source declarations and definitions, its dependency closure,
its callers, its field touchers and its existing Rust consumers. For every pointer field,
argument and return, every code path that stores, transfers, clones, retains or frees it is
inspected.

## 2. Findings

The analysis establishes:

- ownership and transfer direction;
- shared or mutable access;
- nullability;
- scalar, array, or other cardinality;
- type erasure and known element types;
- borrow and keepalive relationships;
- address retention: whether C keeps an object's address beyond the call that receives it,
  to read it, call back with it or free it;
- construction, clone, and destruction paths;
- states and transitions: the states each type's objects pass through, and the calls that
  move them between states, in the orders C allows;
- out-parameters: the pointer arguments a function only writes through;
- string encodings, where a string is known to hold text or a path; and
- failure reporting: the status or sentinel returns and the error state beside the call
  through which a function fails, and the outcomes its callers treat as ordinary.

Observed behaviour overrides names and comments. A distinction the analysis establishes is
preserved in Rust rather than flattened into a copy of an ambiguous C signature.

A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,

hold, and reports which in its final message, as

entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

name: testing-builds
description: "The builds tests run against and how coverage is measured: the prebuilt variants, private builds, coverage instrumentation, objects, suites and figures, and a worklist's coverage. Read before building or choosing a test build, and before measuring or comparing coverage."
---

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those

test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage

with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the

its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as

a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust

#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration

name: testing
description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.

## 4. C tests carried over

The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the
assertions adapted to the safe Rust contract, so that what the C suites established
outlives them. Each names the C test case it carries over, so that before a C test
leaves, at the module's switch or with the exports it calls, the cases none carries
over are listed, and each is carried over or recorded as behaviour the safe API
deliberately changes. A `port/unexport` carries over every C test case that still references the
export it removes, whatever its subject, as a Rust test of that subject, reaching what is
still C through its wrappers, and removes the case from `c/`.

# Testing gates

The gates every landing passes, over the tests [`testing`](../SKILL.md) classifies and the
builds [`testing-builds`](../builds/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Regressions

name: testing
description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."
