# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves
unspecified, such as an iteration order, a message's text, a pointer's value or an
allocation count. A confirmed C defect is not copied into Rust. The divergence is
documented, equivalence tests are retained for the unaffected behaviour, and the
corrected-behaviour regression is a unit test.

`equiv_pub` holds the module's exported API to the C strictly. `equiv_priv` compares an
internal routine with its C counterpart only where one exists, since an idiomatic port may
restructure the internals; a C function the raw bindings do not reach, one with internal
linkage, is compared through the functions that call it.

In a port, equivalence tests are the evidence of a module's migration. While its waves run,
the variants still build its C, which they reach through the raw bindings while the ported
Rust runs under its own names; at its switch they are retired with the C, and the
module evolves as Rust from then on, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes. Only its exports still keep the C contract, which the C tests that stay check.

## 3. Unit tests

A unit test is the right kind when Rust assertions supply the verdict: `unit_pub` on the
public interface, whose tests outlive the C, and `unit_priv` on internal facilities,
including:

- Rust-only `Iterator`, `Debug`, `Clone`, conversions, and builders;
- input rejected by Rust before FFI, including the error and no panic;
- deliberate correction of defective C behaviour;
- unsafe adoption through `from_raw`, `from_ptr`, or similar constructors;
- private or `pub(crate)` constructors and internal destructor/drop plumbing; and
- resource release exercised through any of those raw, unsafe, or internal paths.

## 4. C tests carried over

The `unit_pub` tests the port batches write for a module's items mirror the regression
cases of the C tests tied to it: their inputs, edge cases and call sequences, with the
assertions adapted to the safe Rust contract, so that what the C suites established
outlives them. Each names the C test case it carries over, so that before a C test
leaves, at the module's switch or with the exports it calls, the cases none carries
over are listed, and each is carried over or recorded as behaviour the safe API
deliberately changes. A `port/unexport` carries over every C test case that still references the
export it removes, whatever its subject, as a Rust test of that subject, reaching what is
still C through its wrappers, and removes the case from `c/`.

---
name: versioning
description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."
---

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as

planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Extending

The bindings grow with the batches: a batch whose items need a raw binding the bindings
lack extends its own link unit's input, and nothing else:

1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and
   `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there;
2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on
   the build's configuration, as `crustify_<NAME>`, as
   [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes;
3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and
4. the safe crate is built and tested against them.

Where its link unit's headers name a type another link unit owns, the batch also extends
what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`,
the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link
unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name.

An allowlist or `wrapper.h` change alone leaves the C library as it is, so it reuses a
prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes.

## 5. Landing
6:# Raw bindings
17:## 1. Layout
50:## 2. Generation
116:## 3. Build modes
203:## 4. Extending
224:## 5. Landing
231:## 6. Publishing
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over

---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), before planning an audit's worksets, and when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Worksets

The audit's worksets are planned from a scan of the crate, run once each build
configuration it audits is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of its objectives.
A file outside every configuration scanned has no sites, and is planned from its source.

For `ub`, the modules that hold the smells ffimap's review guidance lists for `ub` are
reviewed first, in that order; for `contracts`, those that hold the crate's unsafe API and
its justifications, the `contracts` counters above. The rest of the crate
follows the smells.

The modules are batched by their sites, and a module that is split keeps a type, trait
impl or function with its sites in one batch. A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`,
`.impl_clone`, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. Each review
runs the same scan over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Worksets

The audit's worksets are planned from a scan of the crate, run once each build
configuration it audits is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of its objectives.
A file outside every configuration scanned has no sites, and is planned from its source.

For `ub`, the modules that hold the smells ffimap's review guidance lists for `ub` are
reviewed first, in that order; for `contracts`, those that hold the crate's unsafe API and
its justifications, the `contracts` counters above. The rest of the crate
follows the smells.

The modules are batched by their sites, and a module that is split keeps a type, trait
impl or function with its sites in one batch. A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`,
`.impl_clone`, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. Each review
runs the same scan over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

---
name: ffibox
description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."
---

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Planning

### Dependencies › Adopted crates

A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists,
each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where
its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses.

## Binding workflow

### Binding workflow › Rust tree

The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on
the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that
each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's
canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of
ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the
compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory.
<!-- TODO: a released ffibox, as a versioned dependency, once `devel` reaches `main`.
Until then the path leaves the crate, against `bindgen`'s Layout section, and pins no
revision. -->

## Binding and porting

Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.

### Binding types

A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.

### Binding types › Safe layout

While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.

### Binding symbols › Functions

A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned
through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's
iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers
## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

## Reviewing

commit 93e0b62edad9ae0bb6f4b68e82f3073d3c4e3f57
Author: Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>
Date:   Fri Nov 13 22:01:00 2026 +0000

    crustify: plan fwrite, a byte-exact write to a shared C stream (planner/run-2)
    
    The side campaign's second advance, for libgit2-crustify's src/cli/opt.c
    before it switches from C. FileRef::print and write_fmt take &str. The
    port's export (cli_opt_status_fprint, wave-186/batch-4) therefore writes
    an argument that is not UTF-8 (--caf\xe9) with U+FFFD where C writes its
    bytes (the parent's crustify/evolution/fileref-prints-bytes, on its
    crustify/waves/wave-186). This run plans what closes that gap and nothing
    else.
    
    Added, modules.json:
    - 5 libio/iofwrite.c, todo: fwrite (_IO_fwrite, weak-aliased), with
      libio/stdio.h's declaration. Its signature reaches _IO_FILE alone, so
      its one record is on libio/genops.c (1 edge, 1 struct). Counters by
      hand, as run 1's: 20 loc in the TU (the function and its 3 alias
      lines), 2 in the API. iolibio.h only declares _IO_fwrite. The
      fwrite_unlocked alias is configured out (_IO_MTSAFE_IO), and the
      unlocked routine is iofwrite_u.c's.
      rust_equivalent: std::io::Write, partial (a Rust-owned sink, not the C
      stream's buffer); no crate, those that bind libc being alternatives to
      the campaign, as run 1 listed them (libc, nix, rustix, relibc,
      cstream 0.1.4, whose io::Write is over fwrite).
    
    schedule.json:
    - module libio/iofwrite.c, layer 1, scheduled after libio/genops.c.
    - appended, todo: wave 5 (libio/iofwrite.c: fwrite, wrap, home
      src/libc/libio/iofwrite.rs), depending on wave 2. No wave re-planned:

/// A C stream as an [`io::Write`], each write one locked `fprintf(stream, "%s", text)` of its
/// bytes, as C's `fprintf` calls write the status message, in order with the C that shares the
/// stream.
///
/// libc's wrapper writes text, a `&str`: bytes that are not UTF-8, which an argument can hold,
/// are written with each invalid sequence replaced by U+FFFD, the one place the export's message
/// departs from C's.
#[cfg(any(test, feature = "ffi-export-src-cli-opt-c"))]
struct FileWriter<'a>(glibc_bindings::libc::libio::genops::FileRef<'a>);

#[cfg(any(test, feature = "ffi-export-src-cli-opt-c"))]
impl io::Write for FileWriter<'_> {
    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
        match core::str::from_utf8(buf) {
            Ok(text) => self.0.print(text)?,
            Err(_) => self.0.print(&String::from_utf8_lossy(buf))?,
        };
        Ok(buf.len())
    }

    /// Nothing: C's `cli_opt_status_fprint` leaves the stream's buffer to its buffering mode.
    fn flush(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.100"
repository = "https://github.com/crustify-rs/glibc-bindings"
license = "LGPL-2.1-or-later"
publish = false

[workspace.dependencies]
bindgen = { version = "=0.73.2", features = ["experimental"] }
cc = "1.5"
ffibox = { git = "https://github.com/crustify-rs/ffibox", rev = "40621a29bffaede7a212c67eeadf803df6f1be29" }
trybuild = "1"
libc-sys = { version = "0.1.0", path = "libc-sys" }

[workspace.metadata.crustify]
nightly = "nightly-2026-10-08"

[workspace.lints.rust]
nonstandard_style = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }
unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "deny"
missing_docs = "warn"
rust_2018_idioms = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
unreachable_pub = "warn"
unused_qualifications = "warn"
unused_lifetimes = "warn"
let_underscore_drop = "warn"
trivial_casts = "warn"
trivial_numeric_casts = "warn"

# crustify — `glibc / libc`

## Settings

As answered in `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md`; a change during the campaign is in its history
and in Notes.

- **source** — `https://sourceware.org/git/glibc.git` @ `ef321e23c2` (`glibc-2.39`); side campaign of `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings` and `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings`
- **campaign** — `wrap`
- **scope** — what `crustify-rs/ffmpeg-bindings` consumes from libc: `struct tm`, `FILE`; what `crustify-rs/libgit2-bindings` consumes: 871 functions, 95 structs, 2 globals, counted per module
- **translate-agent** — `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5.5`, `api`
- **review-agent** — `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5.5`, `api`; objectives `all`
- **plan-agent** — `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5.5`, `api`; `2` runs
- **workload** — max-types `2`, max-syms `25`, max-loc `500`, parallelism `assistant's choice` (from 2026-11-03; `16` before)
- **identity** — author `Marius Momeu <marius.momeu@berkeley.edu>`, co-author `crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>` (from 2026-11-03; `crustify` as the author before)
- **review-workload** — `as many as the reviewed wave requires`
- **sanitizers** — `asan-ubsan`, `tsan`, `bsan`, over the Rust; the system glibc is not instrumented
- **target-config** — none: libc is the system's and is not built, `build.json` version `1`

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total

Deterministic `ffimap <workdir> --json`; no model. Every counter is in the `ffimap.json`
tracked in the campaign's artifact dir, in each wave's `waves/wave-<index>/` and in each
batch run's dir.

### Metrics

| metric | counters | what it counts |
|---|---|---|
| pub raw ptr (safe) | `raw_ptr_pub_safe_interface` | raw pointers on the safe public interface: public fields and safe public fns |
| pub raw ptr | `raw_ptr_pub` | raw pointers anywhere on the public interface, `unsafe fn`s included |
| pub void ptr | `void_ptr_ty_pub_fields_pub` + `void_ptr_fn_pub_safe` + `void_ptr_fn_pub_unsafe` | type-erased pointers left to the API's users |
| pub unsafe fn | `unsafe_fns_pub` | the obligations the crate exports to its callers |
| C borrow | `c_type_borrow_non_sanctioned` | Rust references into C memory outside the sanctioned handle positions; target 0 |
| slice borrow | `raw_ptr_as_slice_borrow` | slices and strings borrowed over raw pointers, which C must neither free nor change |
| unsafe loc % | `unsafe_loc_ratio` | unsafe block lines over code lines; context, not a score |
| unsafe blocks | `unsafe_blocks` | unsafe blocks, the denominator of the ratio's reading |
| Send/Sync | `unsafe_send_impl` + `unsafe_sync_impl` | thread safety asserted rather than derived from the fields |
| C by value | Σ `c_type_by_val_*` + Σ `c_type_std_owner_*` | C types held outside an ffibox owner, which a move can leave dangling |
| Drop/Clone | `drop_impl` + `clone_impl` | lifecycles written by hand rather than through an owner |
| deref outside impl | `raw_ptr_derefs_outside_impl` | raw pointer dereferences outside any `impl` or trait body |

compile-fail cases of the one `compile_fail` test, so the suite's `#[test]` count in
`Coverage stats` does not move. glibc is not built, so every C coverage cell is `—`. The
Rust figure is line coverage over `src/`, measured on the pinned nightly with
`-C instrument-coverage`. `File`'s code is the expansion of ffibox's `define_ctype!`,
which `llvm-cov` counts at the macro's source, outside `src/`, so the batch moves no Rust
figure. `C LoC` stays unmeasured: there is no wavefront database over glibc. `Rust LoC`

`FileRef` derives.

### Wave 2's module pass: `File`'s thread-safety claim

`libio/genops.c`'s only review, `wave-2/batch-1`, judged `File`'s `Send` and `Sync` sound.
They are ffibox's shape for a C object that locks itself: every operation on `FileRef` holds
`flockfile`, and `FileRef` touches nothing of the stream today. The review corrected two
justifications. One was the contract for a borrowed stream, which claimed glibc's own stdio
routines always hold the stream's lock: they skip it on a `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` stream.
The other was `Send for File`'s, which misstated its scope. It also fixed one convention,
an `unsafe_code` expectation on the unit tests, and added a compile-fail case: no `File`
from a stream's layout. Its row's `+LoC` counts those `.rs` changes. Its reports sit in
this table's columns as the dashboard has them: the two `contracts` findings of the
`ffi_import` region under `+internal`, since the dashboard predates the template's
`+contracts import` column. The dashboard also lacks the template's `Module passes` and
`Batches: API stability` tables, which a batch does not add: the module pass fills its row
in the Types tables, and its API measure (`ffimap api diff`) keeps both items. The Rust
coverage was measured again, over `src/`, as the earlier batch measured it: `100.00`% (50
of 50 lines), unchanged, since the landing changes no executable line. No safety-audit
counter moved.

### Wave 3: `fprintf`, written under the stream's lock

`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s wave 3 binds `fprintf` as `FileRef::print(&self, &str) ->
io::Result<usize>`, the fixed-arity form: Rust formats, and the text goes to
`fprintf(stream, "%s", text)` between `flockfile` and `funlockfile`. So it lands in the
stream's own buffer and holds the lock whatever the stream's locking mode. The two lock
routines are raw bindings inside the region, with no API of their own. A `write_fmt` method
beside it lets `write!` format into one locked call, which returns the count as C's does. It
carries no anchor of its own, and `ffimap api` counts it as an extension of `st::_IO_FILE`
and `tdf::FILE`, whose handles it is a method of. `fn::fprintf` is `new`, and the two
unattributed modules are kept. The dashboard has no `Batches: API stability` table to hold
that measure.

The binding clears `errno` before the call and restores it unless the call failed and set
it. glibc returns `-1` without setting `errno` on a wide-oriented stream and when a cookie
stream's write fails silently, as `fmemopen`'s does once its storage is full, so a failure
that leaves `errno` at 0 is an `io::ErrorKind::Other` error with no OS code. The
equivalence suite checks this against C on the same streams.

The row's `+LoC` and `loc` count the regenerated raw bindings (63 lines: `fprintf`,
`flockfile`, `funlockfile`, and the stream routines and constants the tests open streams
with) with the module and the tests. The tests' stream fixture, `tests/fixtures/stream.rs`,
is shared by `unit_pub` and `equiv_pub`. `+UB safe tests` is `+0`: no safe producer of a
`FileRef` exists until wave 4's `stderr`, so the batch's tests open their streams through
the raw bindings. The suite's `-24.28` pp comes from the denominator alone: it covers the same
lines over 86 lines rather than 50. Rust line coverage stays at `100.00`% (86 of 86 lines,
101 of 101 regions; `fprintf.rs` 36 of 36), measured as wave 2's was. Branch coverage is not
instrumented, so no branch figure exists. `EOVERFLOW`, for a text over `INT_MAX` bytes, is the
one C outcome no test reaches, as it needs more than 4 GiB. The safety audit's `unsafe loc %`
(`-6.20` pp) and `unsafe blocks` (`+3`) are the region's three calls. No public `unsafe fn` and
no raw pointer reaches the safe interface.

### Wave 3's module pass: a stream with no lock

`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s only review, `wave-3/batch-1`, judged `FileRef::print` sound on
the points its task named. The lock is released on every path: nothing between `flockfile`
and `funlockfile` can unwind, short of a thread cancellation inside `fprintf`'s write, a
forced unwind Rust does not permit through a frame that owns a `CString`. `errno` is right
on every path the binding reaches, as the `errno-failure-without-errno` proposal now
records. The NUL refusal is the one `binding-symbols` asks of a string. `write_fmt`
correctly carries no anchor, since `conventions` repeats one only for ownership variants
and accessors.

The review found one stream the binding could not take. glibc hands the handler of a
`register_printf_specifier` conversion a stream with a NULL lock, and `flockfile`
dereferences it. The binding now refuses such a stream with `io::ErrorKind::Unsupported`.
That finding is a `contracts` one of the `ffi_import` region, under `+internal`, as wave
2's were. The other finding is a `conventions` one: two `unit_pub` tests called the C
outside the fixture.

The row's `+LoC` and `loc` count the `.rs` changes of `src/` and `tests/`. The
reproducer's 71 lines, under `crustify/reviews/`, are not part of the crate and are left
out. The one test added is a unit test, through a new `unit_pub`-only fixture,

### Wave 4: `stderr`, the first symbol

`libio/stdio.c`'s wave 4 binds the global `stderr` as `stderr() -> FileRef<'static>`, which
reads C's `stderr` on every call, as C's expression does, and borrows the stream it names
for the rest of the program. Its doc states what the `'static` borrow assumes: no write to
`stderr` while another thread may read it, no `fclose` or failing `freopen` of the stream,
and the stream's internal locking left alone. No C of glibc's library or of either parent
breaks these. The raw bindings gain `var stderr`, and the row's `+LoC` counts their 3 lines
with the safe module and the tests. The anchor ``/// Wraps `glb::stderr` `` carries no
`#[doc(alias)]`, because rustc rejects an alias equal to the item's name; proposal
`doc-alias-equal-to-name` covers this. Its tests are 2 `ub_safe`, 2 `unit_pub` and 1
`equiv_pub`, the first `equiv_pub` suite. All of them read the C global, so they carry Miri's
ignore mark. The Rust figures were measured as before, over `src/`, now 54 lines, all
covered. A suite's figure is the share of those 54 lines that suite covers alone. The
safety audit's `unsafe blocks` (+2) are the global's read and the stream's borrow, both in
`ffi_import`. No other metric moved. The API measure, `ffimap api diff`, finds
`glb::stderr` `new` and the other modules `kept`.

### Wave 4's module pass: `stderr` becomes an unsafe accessor

`libio/stdio.c`'s only review, `wave-4/batch-1`, found the safe `stderr() ->
FileRef<'static>` unsound. glibc's `stderr` is a variable its manual lets a program set,
and its example closes a standard stream and points the variable at one `fopen` opened.
`fclose` frees such a stream, so a kept `'static` handle outlives it. The reproducer shows
a heap-use-after-free under ASan from the safe call. The finding is a `contracts` one of the
`ffi_import` region, filed under `+internal` as wave 2's are. The fix makes `stderr` `unsafe
fn stderr<'a>() -> FileRef<'a>`, its `# Safety` section moving onto the caller what the
safe function assumed of the program. `ffimap api diff` classifies `glb::stderr`
`changed`, kept for soundness. `st::_IO_FILE` and `tdf::FILE` are `kept`. The safety audit's
`pub unsafe fn` (+1) is that accessor. No other metric moved. The tests moved with the API:
the two `ub_safe` tests went to a new `ub_unsafe` suite, and the two `unit_pub` tests and
their suite were removed, since `unit_pub` forbids `unsafe_code` and `equiv_pub` asserts the
same against C. `equiv_pub` gained a test that C's reassignment of `stderr` is followed, for
which the raw bindings gain `fopen` and `fclose`, test-only. A compile-fail case keeps the

figure are as measured over `src/` (54 lines) before and after. `stdio.rs`'s 4 lines moved

`100.00`%. The row's `+LoC` counts the Rust tree's `.rs` changes, the regenerated
bindings' 9 lines included. The reproducer's 78 lines, in the reviews dir, are left out.

`-C instrument-coverage`. `File`'s code is the expansion of ffibox's `define_ctype!`,

### Wave 2's module pass: `File`'s thread-safety claim

`libio/genops.c`'s only review, `wave-2/batch-1`, judged `File`'s `Send` and `Sync` sound.
They are ffibox's shape for a C object that locks itself: every operation on `FileRef` holds
`flockfile`, and `FileRef` touches nothing of the stream today. The review corrected two
justifications. One was the contract for a borrowed stream, which claimed glibc's own stdio
routines always hold the stream's lock: they skip it on a `FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER` stream.
The other was `Send for File`'s, which misstated its scope. It also fixed one convention,
an `unsafe_code` expectation on the unit tests, and added a compile-fail case: no `File`
from a stream's layout. Its row's `+LoC` counts those `.rs` changes. Its reports sit in
this table's columns as the dashboard has them: the two `contracts` findings of the
`ffi_import` region under `+internal`, since the dashboard predates the template's
`+contracts import` column. The dashboard also lacks the template's `Module passes` and
`Batches: API stability` tables, which a batch does not add: the module pass fills its row
in the Types tables, and its API measure (`ffimap api diff`) keeps both items. The Rust
coverage was measured again, over `src/`, as the earlier batch measured it: `100.00`% (50
of 50 lines), unchanged, since the landing changes no executable line. No safety-audit
counter moved.

### Wave 3: `fprintf`, written under the stream's lock

`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s wave 3 binds `fprintf` as `FileRef::print(&self, &str) ->
io::Result<usize>`, the fixed-arity form: Rust formats, and the text goes to
`fprintf(stream, "%s", text)` between `flockfile` and `funlockfile`. So it lands in the
stream's own buffer and holds the lock whatever the stream's locking mode. The two lock
routines are raw bindings inside the region, with no API of their own. A `write_fmt` method
beside it lets `write!` format into one locked call, which returns the count as C's does. It
carries no anchor of its own, and `ffimap api` counts it as an extension of `st::_IO_FILE`
and `tdf::FILE`, whose handles it is a method of. `fn::fprintf` is `new`, and the two
unattributed modules are kept. The dashboard has no `Batches: API stability` table to hold
that measure.

The binding clears `errno` before the call and restores it unless the call failed and set
it. glibc returns `-1` without setting `errno` on a wide-oriented stream and when a cookie
stream's write fails silently, as `fmemopen`'s does once its storage is full, so a failure
that leaves `errno` at 0 is an `io::ErrorKind::Other` error with no OS code. The
equivalence suite checks this against C on the same streams.

The row's `+LoC` and `loc` count the regenerated raw bindings (63 lines: `fprintf`,
`flockfile`, `funlockfile`, and the stream routines and constants the tests open streams
with) with the module and the tests. The tests' stream fixture, `tests/fixtures/stream.rs`,
is shared by `unit_pub` and `equiv_pub`. `+UB safe tests` is `+0`: no safe producer of a
`FileRef` exists until wave 4's `stderr`, so the batch's tests open their streams through
the raw bindings. The suite's `-24.28` pp comes from the denominator alone: it covers the same
lines over 86 lines rather than 50. Rust line coverage stays at `100.00`% (86 of 86 lines,
101 of 101 regions; `fprintf.rs` 36 of 36), measured as wave 2's was. Branch coverage is not
instrumented, so no branch figure exists. `EOVERFLOW`, for a text over `INT_MAX` bytes, is the
one C outcome no test reaches, as it needs more than 4 GiB. The safety audit's `unsafe loc %`
(`-6.20` pp) and `unsafe blocks` (`+3`) are the region's three calls. No public `unsafe fn` and
no raw pointer reaches the safe interface.

### Wave 3's module pass: a stream with no lock

`stdio-common/fprintf.c`'s only review, `wave-3/batch-1`, judged `FileRef::print` sound on
the points its task named. The lock is released on every path: nothing between `flockfile`
and `funlockfile` can unwind, short of a thread cancellation inside `fprintf`'s write, a
forced unwind Rust does not permit through a frame that owns a `CString`. `errno` is right
on every path the binding reaches, as the `errno-failure-without-errno` proposal now
records. The NUL refusal is the one `binding-symbols` asks of a string. `write_fmt`
correctly carries no anchor, since `conventions` repeats one only for ownership variants
and accessors.

The review found one stream the binding could not take. glibc hands the handler of a
`register_printf_specifier` conversion a stream with a NULL lock, and `flockfile`
dereferences it. The binding now refuses such a stream with `io::ErrorKind::Unsupported`.
That finding is a `contracts` one of the `ffi_import` region, under `+internal`, as wave
2's were. The other finding is a `conventions` one: two `unit_pub` tests called the C
outside the fixture.

The row's `+LoC` and `loc` count the `.rs` changes of `src/` and `tests/`. The
reproducer's 71 lines, under `crustify/reviews/`, are not part of the crate and are left
out. The one test added is a unit test, through a new `unit_pub`-only fixture,
`tests/fixtures/stream_unit.rs`. Rust line coverage stays at `100.00`% (96 of 96 lines, 109
of 109 regions; `fprintf.rs` 46 of 46), measured as wave 2's was. llvm-cov counts std's
`thread_local` code, which the fixture instantiates, under the toolchain's sources, and the
measure leaves it out. The `UB safe` (`-3.51` pp) and `equiv` (`+2.14` pp) moves come
from the new lines alone: the equivalence suite reaches `has_lock` on every stream. The
`Rust LoC` line moved by the delta of one counter run over the base and the landed tree,
`+10` non-test and `+90` test lines. That counter does not reproduce the earlier absolute
figures exactly. The safety audit's `+1` unsafe block is `has_lock`'s read of `_lock`.
`ffimap api diff` keeps `fn::fprintf` (`kept`) and both unattributed modules.


### Wave 4: `stderr`, the first symbol

`libio/stdio.c`'s wave 4 binds the global `stderr` as `stderr() -> FileRef<'static>`, which
reads C's `stderr` on every call, as C's expression does, and borrows the stream it names
for the rest of the program. Its doc states what the `'static` borrow assumes: no write to
`stderr` while another thread may read it, no `fclose` or failing `freopen` of the stream,
and the stream's internal locking left alone. No C of glibc's library or of either parent
breaks these. The raw bindings gain `var stderr`, and the row's `+LoC` counts their 3 lines
with the safe module and the tests. The anchor ``/// Wraps `glb::stderr` `` carries no
`#[doc(alias)]`, because rustc rejects an alias equal to the item's name; proposal
`doc-alias-equal-to-name` covers this. Its tests are 2 `ub_safe`, 2 `unit_pub` and 1
`equiv_pub`, the first `equiv_pub` suite. All of them read the C global, so they carry Miri's
ignore mark. The Rust figures were measured as before, over `src/`, now 54 lines, all
covered. A suite's figure is the share of those 54 lines that suite covers alone. The
safety audit's `unsafe blocks` (+2) are the global's read and the stream's borrow, both in
`ffi_import`. No other metric moved. The API measure, `ffimap api diff`, finds
`glb::stderr` `new` and the other modules `kept`.

### Wave 4's module pass: `stderr` becomes an unsafe accessor

`libio/stdio.c`'s only review, `wave-4/batch-1`, found the safe `stderr() ->
FileRef<'static>` unsound. glibc's `stderr` is a variable its manual lets a program set,
and its example closes a standard stream and points the variable at one `fopen` opened.
`fclose` frees such a stream, so a kept `'static` handle outlives it. The reproducer shows
a heap-use-after-free under ASan from the safe call. The finding is a `contracts` one of the
`ffi_import` region, filed under `+internal` as wave 2's are. The fix makes `stderr` `unsafe
fn stderr<'a>() -> FileRef<'a>`, its `# Safety` section moving onto the caller what the
safe function assumed of the program. `ffimap api diff` classifies `glb::stderr`
`changed`, kept for soundness. `st::_IO_FILE` and `tdf::FILE` are `kept`. The safety audit's
`pub unsafe fn` (+1) is that accessor. No other metric moved. The tests moved with the API:
the two `ub_safe` tests went to a new `ub_unsafe` suite, and the two `unit_pub` tests and
their suite were removed, since `unit_pub` forbids `unsafe_code` and `equiv_pub` asserts the
same against C. `equiv_pub` gained a test that C's reassignment of `stderr` is followed, for
which the raw bindings gain `fopen` and `fclose`, test-only. A compile-fail case keeps the
safe call rejected. Hence the tests row's negative cells: each suite's count and Rust
figure are as measured over `src/` (54 lines) before and after. `stdio.rs`'s 4 lines moved
from the `ub_safe` and `unit_pub` runs to `ub_unsafe`'s, and the joint figure stays
`100.00`%. The row's `+LoC` counts the Rust tree's `.rs` changes, the regenerated
bindings' 9 lines included. The reproducer's 78 lines, in the reviews dir, are left out.

### Integration of `stdio-common/fprintf.c` after `libio/stdio.c`

The merge keeps every row both modules added. The `Σ` rows of the Symbols tables and the
Overview's `Rust LoC` are ours plus theirs less the merge base's; the Coverage stats' counts
are the merged suites', with `fprintf.c`'s percentages, the later landing's, and `stdio.c`'s
for `ub_unsafe`, until a gate measures the merged tree.

fprintf.c: wrap 1 item (wave-3/batch-0/run-1)

fn::fprintf

fprintf is bound through its fixed-arity form, FileRef::print(&self,
&str) -> io::Result<usize>: Rust formats, and the text goes to
fprintf(stream, "%s", text), so that it lands in the buffer the C that
shares the stream writes. The call holds the stream's lock throughout:
flockfile before it, funlockfile after errno is read, whatever the
stream's locking mode. That keeps FileRef's Send and Sync sound on a
FSETLOCKING_BYCALLER stream, which glibc's own fprintf would not lock.
flockfile and funlockfile are raw bindings inside the region, with no
API of their own. FileRef::write_fmt lets write! format into one such
call, returning the count as C does.

errno is cleared before the call and restored unless the call failed
and set it. glibc fails without setting errno on a wide-oriented stream
and when a cookie stream's write fails silently, so such a failure is an
io::ErrorKind::Other error with no OS code, not a stale errno. A NUL in
the text is refused as InvalidInput before the call.

The raw bindings gain fprintf, flockfile and funlockfile, and the stream
routines and constants the tests open their streams with (<stdio_ext.h>
and <wchar.h> join wrapper.h). Tests: 6 equivalence tests against the
raw fprintf on growing, fixed, read-only, full, by-caller-locked and
wide streams, and 16 unit tests (3 inline). They cover the lock held
across threads and released on every outcome, and errno on every path.
They run plain and under ASan, the threaded ones under TSan, and two
under BSan. The Rust tests run under Miri; those that call C are marked
after each was seen to stop there. ub_safe gains none: no safe producer
of a FileRef exists before wave 4's stderr.

Proposal filed: errno-failure-without-errno. stream-lock-for-shared-
writes landed as its private-binding alternative; ffibox-ref-contract-
self-locking gains this batch's use as evidence. Lessons: threaded
stream tests use a file stream under TSan; ASan's doctests need
RUSTDOCFLAGS.
